overview.Module Title: Fairness in Everyday Life: A Comparative Thinking Module

sections.Aims and Fit of Module: This module explores how cultures and societies across the world have understood ideas related to equality, fairness, solidarity, and social responsibility. Using short philosophical ideas, cultural perspectives, proverbs, and examples from public life and media, students compare how different societies understand and discuss shared social questions. Weekly topics are organised around comparative questions. Through discussion, comparison, and reflective analysis, students develop intercultural awareness, analytical thinking, and communication skills. The module emphasises comparison, perspective, and discussion rather than any single definition of equality, encouraging students to consider how social values and public expectations differ across cultures and communities. The module sits within the Semester 1 exploratory interdisciplinary block. It supports transition into English-medium university learning by developing analytical, communicative, and intercultural skills through collaborative inquiry and reflective discussion. The module is suitable for students from a wide range of disciplinary pathways who wish to develop comparative, intercultural, and discussion-based approaches to exploring contemporary social questions and building foundational skills for academic progression.
sections.Learning outcomes: A Identify and compare how different cultures and societies understand equality, fairness, and social responsibility. B Analyse how social values, public expectations, and cultural perspectives influence responses to shared social questions in different contexts. C Use examples from media and everyday life to develop and communicate comparative perspectives through discussion and reflection, building confidence in academic expression and collaboration in English-medium contexts.
sections.Method of teaching and learning: The module uses a combination of short introductory inputs, comparative activities, discussion, and reflective analysis. Weekly topics are organised around comparative questions, drawing on philosophical ideas, cultural perspectives, proverbs, and contemporary examples from public life and media. Through comparison and discussion, students explore different responses to shared social questions and consider how social values and public expectations vary across cultures and communities. The module emphasises perspective, comparison, and reflection rather than any single definition of equality. The module is co-delivered with LIFE through the common Semester 1 Academic Horizons spine. School staff provide the social and cultural context, challenge framing, disciplinary credibility, and assessment of the academic project output. LIFE staff support the inquiry process, responsible AI/digital practice, teamwork, reflection, feedback use, and pathway alignment activities.
